En algunas palabras de cora que tienen más de una sílaba, hay que indicar cuál sílaba está acentuada. La sílaba se marca con un acento (´) sobre la vocal, como en las siguientes palabras: cáanarij 'ropa' — canárij 'guitarra'. ... Lee en voz alta cada uno de los siguientes pares de palabras en cora, y escucha la diferencia de pronunciación y el cambio de significado que causa el acento. mɨ́'ɨchi 'está muerto' / mɨ'ɨchí 'un muerto'; tyéetye 'granizo' / tyetyéj 'piedra'; cáanarij 'ropa' / canárij 'guitarra'; náavi 'hormiga' / navíj 'cuero'.

new_statements.translation: This lesson presents the accent. A syllable is accented when it is pronounced with more force and has a higher pitch than the other syllables in the word. In some Cora words that have more than one syllable, it is necessary to indicate which syllable is accented. The syllable is marked with an accent (´) over the vowel, as in the following words: cáanarij 'clothes' — canárij 'guitar'. Read aloud each of the following pairs of Cora words and listen to the difference in pronunciation and the change of meaning that the accent causes: mɨ́'ɨchi 'he is dead' / mɨ'ɨchí 'a dead person'; tyéetye 'hail' / tyetyéj 'stone'; cáanarij 'clothes' / canárij 'guitar'; náavi 'ant' / navíj 'leather'.

new_statements.rule_in_words: Word accent (realised as greater force plus higher pitch) is not predictable from position: its place must be written with an acute on polysyllables, and pairs of words are distinguished solely by which syllable carries it (initial vs. second/final), including grammatical pairs ('he is dead' vs 'a dead person'). No default position is stated; in practice the orthography marks the accent on essentially every polysyllabic word.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Nothing said (Casad 1984:157, for the Jesús María dialect, mentions primary and secondary degrees of stress alongside phonemic tone).
new_statements.exceptions: None; the book only says accent must be indicated 'in some words of more than one syllable' without saying which words go unmarked.
new_statements.domain_note: Word-level, citation forms in a literacy primer; the description bundles intensity and high pitch ('tono más alto'), consistent with the tone/pitch accent-plus-stress analysis Casad 1984 gives for the sister Jesús María variety (tone attraction to preposed articles etc. is a phrase-level effect there).
new_statements.identity_note: The quoted source describes the Santa Teresa (tereseño) variety proper, i.e. the name-giving dialect of sant1424 / ISO cok (authors from Santa Teresa, Municipio del Nayar). Parker's 2018 MA and ELAR deposit concern San Juan Corapan (Corapeño), which Ethnologue/ELAR also file under cok. Casad 1984 (also saved here) is the Jesús María dialect = El Nayar Cora, elna1235/crn, and must not be used as a first-hand sant1424 statement; McMahon 1959/1967 are Presidio de los Reyes (crn).

sources.note: Lección 9 'El acento' (p.47): an accented syllable is pronounced with more force and higher pitch; in polysyllabic words the accented syllable must be indicated with an acute; minimal pairs differing only in accent placement (cáanarij 'ropa' / canárij 'guitarra'; mɨ́'ɨchi 'está muerto' / mɨ'ɨchí 'un muerto'; tyéetye 'granizo' / tyetyéj 'piedra'; náavi 'hormiga' / navíj 'cuero'). No default-position rule stated; accent written on virtually every polysyllable throughout the book.

sources.note: Describes the JESÚS MARÍA (El Nayar, elna1235/crn) dialect, not Santa Teresa. p.157: 'Tone is phonemic and operates partly independently of stress, which can be analyzed into primary and secondary degrees.' pp.167-168 'Tone': tone attraction, tone placement distinguishing SG/PL (cé'epe/ce'epé) and grammatical class (mɨ́'ɨčî 'He's dead' / mɨ'ɨčí 'A dead person'), no rule for stress position. Intro p.155 names Dolores–Santa Teresa as the third principal dialect area but gives no data for it.
